yes_case.case: The closest past episodes are the 2018 imposition of GST on priority sector lending (PSL) certificate transactions and the 2022 decision to withdraw exemptions on financial services provided by intermediaries to banks. In both prior episodes, the GST Council acted swiftly to plug perceived tax arbitrage loopholes in business-to-business (B2B) financial intermediation once revenue leakage became apparent. This current episode differs crucially from the 2018 PSL certificate case because co-lending arrangements involve direct, ongoing operational integration and loan administration between NBFCs and commercial banks, creating a much larger and more visible volume of fee-based transactions. It differs from the 2022 intermediary ruling because the scale of co-lending has expanded exponentially since then, shifting the Council's focus from minor compliance clarifications to a major systemic tax harmonization effort. These specific historical precedents of closing loopholes in inter-institutional financial services make an 18% GST approval on NBFC-to-bank services a continuation of established fiscal policy.

The 2022 GST Council clarification regarding financial intermediary services and bank outsourcing fees.
The structural reliance on fee-sharing and servicing charges inherent in modern NBFC-bank co-lending models.

no_case.case: The closest past historical episodes involving complex financial sector tax clarifications—specifically the disputes over taxation of corporate guarantees and the initial ambiguity around inter-corporate guarantees under GST—differ fundamentally from the current NBFC-to-bank co-lending scenario. In those past episodes, the services were direct bilateral transactions with clear counterparties and easily identifiable valuation mechanisms. By contrast, the proposed 18% GST on NBFC services to banks under co-lending involves tripartite risk-sharing, blended interest rates, and complex pass-through fee structures that do not cleanly map onto standard intermediary or facilitation services. In past tax clarification episodes, the economic impact was largely confined to single corporate balance sheets, whereas applying an 18% levy to co-lending structures directly threatens the operational viability of financial inclusion models mandated by central regulators, introducing systemic friction that historical tax rulings never had to navigate.

advocate.why_it_could_be_wrong: Complex financial sector taxation issues involving co-lending models require extensive consultations between the GST Law Committee, the Ministry of Finance, and the RBI. In the absence of visible telltale signs (such as Fitment Committee draft notes or agenda inclusion), technical tax proposals on banking friction usually stall for multiple meeting cycles or get deferred to avoid disrupting priority sector lending.
advocate.move_reason: The aggregate median (55.0%) is overly anchored on broad historical pass rates for GST Council measures (actor_incentive at 75%, reference_class at 68%). It under-weights procedural realities (mechanism_calendar at 22%, telltale at 14%), which show that specialized financial tax tweaks rarely pass without prior public committee vetting.
advocate.concerns: The top-line aggregate assumes high intent translates directly to execution, ignoring the procedural chokepoints of GST Council agendas where non-publicized technical changes routinely lag behind high-profile rate rationalization efforts.
